```{r setup}
library(mixtureEM)
```

## Why a reporting function

Sorgente et al. (2025) read 313 latent class analyses published in psychology
between 2014 and 2024 and checked them against what the tutorials say a paper
should report. Most papers left out the basics: 23% named the estimator, 16%
said how many random starts they used, 17% said how missing data were
handled, and 1.6% shared their code. Van de Schoot et al. (2017) found the same
pattern in trajectory studies: of 38 papers, one reported its number of random
starts.

None of this is hard to report. The fitted model already holds every one of
those numbers; they are just spread over `print()`, `summary()`,
`class_sizes()` and the comparison table. `report_methods()` collects them
into the paragraphs a methods section needs, and `grolts_report()` walks the
GRoLTS checklist for trajectory models. Neither function computes anything new,
and neither grades the result: no sentence calls an entropy "good" or a class
"too small". Those judgements need the substantive context the function does
not have.

## A latent class analysis, from enumeration to methods section

The `ventura_leon` data hold 16 binary infidelity items for 400 young adults
(see `vignette("ventura_leon")`). Compare one to four classes:

```{r enumerate}
items <- as.matrix(ventura_leon[, 7:22])
cmp <- compare_mixtures(items, k_range = 1:4, measurement = "binary",
                        n_init = 20, random_state = 1)
```

Passing the comparison to `report_methods()` writes up the model with the
lowest BIC, plus a paragraph on the enumeration itself: the range of K, whether
the one-class model was in it (a common omission), the indices reported and
which K the BIC picked.

```{r report}
report_methods(cmp)
```

Each paragraph is one element of a character vector, so you can paste them
into a manuscript one at a time, or edit them first. The references are kept
in `attr(, "references")` and printed once at the end, which works for both
author-year and numbered citation styles.

Two things the report tells you are worth acting on before you write:

- **Whether the best log-likelihood was replicated.** If the paragraph says it
  was reached by one start only, refit with more starts (`n_init = 100`) and
  check that nothing better appears (`vignette("estimation")`).
- **Whether the sample you analysed is the one you collected.** Cases with no
  observed indicator are removed before estimation, and the first paragraph
  says how many.

To describe a different K than the BIC's choice, pass `k`:
`report_methods(cmp, k = 3)`. The enumeration paragraph then says that the
reported model is not the lowest-BIC one.

## A trajectory model and the GRoLTS checklist

`grolts_report()` takes a growth model from `fit_gmm()` or `fit_lcga()`, or a
`compare_longitudinal()` comparison of them, and sorts the 21 GRoLTS items into
three groups: those the fit answers, those you must supply, and those that do
not apply to the model. Here is a small simulated example with two trajectory
classes over four occasions:

```{r grolts}
set.seed(5)
y <- matrix(rnorm(800, sd = 1), 200) +
  outer(rep(c(0, 1.5), each = 100), 0:3, function(a, t) a + (a / 2) * t)
traj <- compare_longitudinal(y, k_range = 1:3, model = "lcga", times = 4,
                             family = "gaussian", n_init = 5,
                             random_state = 1, verbose = FALSE)
grolts_report(traj)
```

The "you must supply" group is the useful part. It lists what no fit can know:
how much measurement times varied within a wave, why the data are missing,
which other model shapes you tried and why you kept this one, and the plots a
reader needs to see.

The function prints no score such as "15 of 21". A count treats the items as
interchangeable, and they are not; which gaps matter depends on what the paper
claims.

## References

Masyn, K. E. (2013). Latent class analysis and finite mixture modeling. In
T. D. Little (Ed.), *The Oxford Handbook of Quantitative Methods* (Vol. 2,
pp. 551-611). Oxford University Press.

Sorgente, A., Caliciuri, R., Robba, M., Lanz, M., & Zumbo, B. D. (2025). A
systematic review of latent class analysis in psychology: Examining the gap
between guidelines and research practice. *Behavior Research Methods*, *57*,
301.

van de Schoot, R., Sijbrandij, M., Winter, S. D., Depaoli, S., & Vermunt, J. K.
(2017). The GRoLTS-checklist: Guidelines for reporting on latent trajectory
studies. *Structural Equation Modeling*, *24*(3), 451-467.
<https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2016.1247646>
